messages.subject: Doubts about the SEM
parts:
Hi everyone, 

I am quite new to SEM and also lavaan, and I would like to use them to analyze my data. The idea of my study is that, I have many measured variables using three subspecies of plants and I want to use these variables to distinguish/predict the plant subspecies. I read the tutorial and some papers about SEM and lavaan, however, I am not sure can I do this with lavaan. I am thinking of two ways for my purpose, one is kind of piecewise comparisons, that is, including two subspecies for each model and run three models to compare all combinations; another one is that use the subspecies as the group and obtain three SEM, with probably different loadings of variables for each model.

Could you please help me with my problems and any advice is appreciated greatly.

Best,
Wenyong

messages.subject: Re: Doubts about the SEM
parts: The idea of my study is that, I have many measured variables using three subspecies of plants and I want to use these variables to distinguish/predict the plant subspecies.

So you have a single nominal outcome (plant subspecies A, B, or C), and you want to use other variables to predict that?  This sounds like you need a multinomial logistic regression, not SEM.

Terry

Thanks again!

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Doubts about the SEM
parts: Besides prediction, I also want to test is there any causal-effects within the variables and with the outcome (subspecises), i.e., which variables contribute/decide to the differences among them. I think SEM could be a way for this aim, but just don't know how to organize the analysis.

It sounds like you might consider your plant characteristics as indicators of subspecies, which could be considered a categorical latent variable.  Look into latent class analysis and latent profile analysis, which unfortunately will not be available in lavaan for some time.  the R package "nlsem" can fit finite mixture models, but if you are a novice in SEM, using that package might be an uphill battle (but worth the effort, if that is what you want to do).  In Mplus, you could fit 2 latent class models: one with known classes (since it seems you already have that variable recorded) and one with unknown classes, to see how closely the results align with your known classes.  There might be some other validation methods I'm unaware of -- I am not experienced with latent class models.  If you can't locate any satisfactory literature on fitting latent class models, you could post your question on SEMNET for help.  If you have an Mplus license, their forum could also provide help fitting your model (again, if that is indeed the type of model you want to fit).

Terry
